raw_evidence.label: Origin of Sechselaeuten and the Boeoegg ritual
raw_evidence.content: Sechselaeuten is Zurich's spring guild festival, traced to a 1525 city-council decision that summer working hours would end at six bells instead of five. The pyre-and-effigy ritual in its modern form dates to 1902, when the parade was combined with the official Boeoegg burn. Since 1892 the figure has resembled a snowman, standing for winter being driven out by spring. Today the Boeoegg is roughly 3.40 m tall, weighs about 80 kg, is made of jute, wood-wool and cardboard, has roughly 100 firework charges packed into its head, and sits atop a 10-metre wood pyre lit at exactly 6 p.m. on the third Monday of April. The CSV used here covers 1923-2025 and was assembled by Phil Shem from official Zurich sources, then merged with MeteoSwiss summer climate data by Matt for TidyTuesday week 2025-12-02.

raw_evidence.label: The folk-science claim: faster burn predicts hotter summer
raw_evidence.content: The popular saying is simple and beloved: the quicker the Boeoegg's head explodes, the finer the coming summer will be. A long, smoldering burn is read as a portent of cold and rain. The claim has been repeated in Swiss media since at least the early 20th century and is the entire reason the dataset's burn-duration column carries any meaning at all. The festival treats the snowman's head explosion as a one-shot annual forecast for the June-August Swiss Plateau weather. This folk forecast is what the dataset is trying to test against MeteoSwiss climate measurements.

raw_evidence.label: Record extremes in burn duration
raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains both extremes Swiss media routinely cite. The shortest official burn on record is 5 minutes 7 seconds, set in 1974 (recorded as 5.12 minutes in this CSV). The longest is 57 minutes, set in 2023 - a notoriously slow, smoldering burn that drew live-TV jokes about whether the head would explode at all. These extremes anchor the duration distribution and provide natural narrative bookends.

raw_evidence.label: Extremes - shortest and longest burns
raw_evidence.content: The shortest five burns are 4.00 min (1956), 5.00 (1971), 5.00 (1968), 5.12 (1974) and 5.70 (2003). The longest five are 40.00 (1988), 40.00 (1970), 43.57 (2016), 57.00 (2023) and 60.00 (1923). Of the five fastest, only 2003 was a record-hot summer (21.67 deg C); the other four were ordinary. Of the five slowest, only 2023 was a record summer - 57 minutes of smoldering before a 20.07 deg C summer. The two extremes that frame the dataset (1956 at 4 min, 1923 at 60 min) sit on opposite ends of the duration scale but were both followed by below-average summers (15.07 and 16.67 deg C respectively).

raw_evidence.label: MeteoSwiss verdict: no significant correlation
raw_evidence.content: Switzerland's national meteorological office, MeteoSwiss, has analyzed the burn-time series against subsequent summer temperatures on the Swiss Plateau and concluded there is no significant correlation between the two. Their public page states the Boeoegg's predictive value cannot be scientifically supported, calling the snowman a 'very poor forecaster' and contrasting it with the agency's own seasonal climate model, which does show statistically significant correlation with observed summer temperatures. MeteoSwiss attributes the noise to physical factors that have nothing to do with future weather: pyre construction, firewood humidity, the type and amount of accelerant used, and weather on the day of Sechselaeuten itself.

raw_evidence.label: Pearson correlations: burn duration vs each climate variable
raw_evidence.content: Across 65 paired observations, the Pearson correlation between burn duration and the headline climate variable - summer mean temperature (tre200m0) - is just r = 0.194, with p = 0.121, not statistically significant. The folk rule predicts a NEGATIVE correlation (faster burn = hotter summer); the data shows a weak POSITIVE one (slower burn associates very mildly with hotter summers). The only correlation that reaches conventional significance is duration vs absolute summer maximum temperature (tre200mx) at r = 0.276, p = 0.026, again positive. Sunshine totals (r = 0.168) and sunshine percentage (r = 0.170) are also non-significant; precipitation is r = -0.113 and non-significant. Across all six climate variables, none supports the folk-science direction.

raw_evidence.label: Folk-rule split test: fast burns vs slow burns
raw_evidence.content: Splitting the 65 burns at the median (13 min), the folk rule predicts the 32 fast-burn years should be hotter than the 33 slow-burn years. They are not. The fast group's mean summer temperature is 17.49 deg C; the slow group's is 17.64 deg C - a difference of -0.148 deg C in the wrong direction. The Welch t-test gives t = -0.45, p = 0.66, indistinguishable from zero. Just as starkly, only 2 of the 32 fast-burn years (6.3%) were record summers, while 8 of the 33 slow-burn years (24.2%) were. By the only criterion the folk rule cares about, slow burns predict record summers four times more often than fast burns do.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_07: How well does the folk rule (faster = hotter) classify record summers? ---
print("=== ana_07 ===")
# A "fast" burn = below the median duration. Folk rule predicts those years should be hotter.
median_dur = df["duration"].median()
fast = df[df["duration"] < median_dur]
slow = df[df["duration"] >= median_dur]
print(f"median duration cutoff: {median_dur:.2f} min")
print(f"fast burns (n={len(fast)}): mean summer T = {fast['tre200m0'].mean():.2f}C, record summers = {fast['record'].sum()}/{len(fast)}")
print(f"slow burns (n={len(slow)}): mean summer T = {slow['tre200m0'].mean():.2f}C, record summers = {slow['record'].sum()}/{len(slow)}")
print(f"diff in mean T (fast - slow): {fast['tre200m0'].mean() - slow['tre200m0'].mean():.3f}C")
t_test = stats.ttest_ind(fast["tre200m0"], slow["tre200m0"], equal_var=False)
print(f"Welch t-test on mean summer T: t={t_test.statistic:.2f}, p={t_test.pvalue:.4f}")

raw_evidence.content: Treating fast burns as a folk-rule prediction of a record summer, the confusion matrix shows 25 true negatives, 30 false alarms, 8 misses, and just 2 hits. The folk rule is roughly half as accurate as just saying nothing - it has informative value below noise.

total = len(df)
correct = int(ct.loc[True, True]) + int(ct.loc[False, False])
print(f"agreement: {correct}/{total} = {correct/total*100:.1f}%")

base = (df["record"] == False).sum()  # noqa: E712
print(f"base-rate accuracy of always saying 'not record': {base}/{total} = {base/total*100:.1f}%")

raw_evidence.label: Folk-rule split test: fast burns vs slow burns
raw_evidence.content: Splitting the 65 burns at the median (13 min), the folk rule predicts the 32 fast-burn years should be hotter than the 33 slow-burn years. They are not. The fast group's mean summer temperature is 17.49 deg C; the slow group's is 17.64 deg C - a difference of -0.148 deg C in the wrong direction. The Welch t-test gives t = -0.45, p = 0.66, indistinguishable from zero. Just as starkly, only 2 of the 32 fast-burn years (6.3%) were record summers, while 8 of the 33 slow-burn years (24.2%) were. By the only criterion the folk rule cares about, slow burns predict record summers four times more often than fast burns do.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_07: How well does the folk rule (faster = hotter) classify record summers? ---
print("=== ana_07 ===")
# A "fast" burn = below the median duration. Folk rule predicts those years should be hotter.
median_dur = df["duration"].median()
fast = df[df["duration"] < median_dur]
slow = df[df["duration"] >= median_dur]
print(f"median duration cutoff: {median_dur:.2f} min")
print(f"fast burns (n={len(fast)}): mean summer T = {fast['tre200m0'].mean():.2f}C, record summers = {fast['record'].sum()}/{len(fast)}")
print(f"slow burns (n={len(slow)}): mean summer T = {slow['tre200m0'].mean():.2f}C, record summers = {slow['record'].sum()}/{len(slow)}")
print(f"diff in mean T (fast - slow): {fast['tre200m0'].mean() - slow['tre200m0'].mean():.3f}C")
t_test = stats.ttest_ind(fast["tre200m0"], slow["tre200m0"], equal_var=False)
print(f"Welch t-test on mean summer T: t={t_test.statistic:.2f}, p={t_test.pvalue:.4f}")

raw_evidence.label: Record extremes in burn duration
raw_evidence.content: The dataset contains both extremes Swiss media routinely cite. The shortest official burn on record is 5 minutes 7 seconds, set in 1974 (recorded as 5.12 minutes in this CSV). The longest is 57 minutes, set in 2023 - a notoriously slow, smoldering burn that drew live-TV jokes about whether the head would explode at all. These extremes anchor the duration distribution and provide natural narrative bookends.

raw_evidence.label: Why burn time is mostly noise: physical confounders
raw_evidence.content: The mechanism MeteoSwiss invokes for why burn duration tells you nothing about July is straightforward physics. Each year the pyre is freshly built; the firewood is bought from different suppliers and stored differently, so its moisture content varies. The weather on the festival afternoon - wind, rain, ambient temperature - shifts how flames climb the wood stack. The amount of fire accelerant the guild uses is a direct lever on speed-of-ignition. And the head is packed with about 100 explosive charges whose ignition order depends on how the heat front reaches them. None of these factors carries information about the upcoming June-August jet stream over the Alps, so any correlation that does emerge is dominated by these confounders.

raw_evidence.label: Long-run trend in Boeoegg burn duration (and decadal pattern)
raw_evidence.content: The headline regression of duration on year is statistically inconclusive: slope +0.0756 min/year, r = 0.136, p = 0.281. But the decadal medians tell a clearer story than the slope. The 1950s-60s averaged 6-11 min burns, the 1970s-80s averaged 17-21 min, the 1990s and 2000s drifted back down to roughly 10-15 min, and the 2020s have so far averaged 33.6 min - more than five times the 1950s. This is the period MeteoSwiss flags as having loose, smoldering pyres rather than a meaningful climate signal.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_11: Linear trend in burn duration 1923-2025 ---
print("\n=== ana_11 ===")
ddf = df.dropna(subset=["duration"]).copy()
slope2, intercept2, r2, p2, se2 = stats.linregress(ddf["year"], ddf["duration"])
print(f"n = {len(ddf)}")
print(f"slope: {slope2:.4f} min/year   r = {r2:.3f}   p = {p2:.4f}")
print(f"100-year change implied by slope: {slope2*100:.2f} min")
# decadal means of duration
ddf["decade"] = (ddf["year"] // 10) * 10
dec = ddf.groupby("decade")["duration"].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]).round(2)
print("decadal means/medians:")
print(dec)

raw_evidence.label: Long-run trend in Boeoegg burn duration (and decadal pattern)
raw_evidence.content: The headline regression of duration on year is statistically inconclusive: slope +0.0756 min/year, r = 0.136, p = 0.281. But the decadal medians tell a clearer story than the slope. The 1950s-60s averaged 6-11 min burns, the 1970s-80s averaged 17-21 min, the 1990s and 2000s drifted back down to roughly 10-15 min, and the 2020s have so far averaged 33.6 min - more than five times the 1950s. This is the period MeteoSwiss flags as having loose, smoldering pyres rather than a meaningful climate signal.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_11: Linear trend in burn duration 1923-2025 ---
print("\n=== ana_11 ===")
ddf = df.dropna(subset=["duration"]).copy()
slope2, intercept2, r2, p2, se2 = stats.linregress(ddf["year"], ddf["duration"])
print(f"n = {len(ddf)}")
print(f"slope: {slope2:.4f} min/year   r = {r2:.3f}   p = {p2:.4f}")
print(f"100-year change implied by slope: {slope2*100:.2f} min")
# decadal means of duration
ddf["decade"] = (ddf["year"] // 10) * 10
dec = ddf.groupby("decade")["duration"].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]).round(2)
print("decadal means/medians:")
print(dec)

raw_evidence.label: Why burn time is mostly noise: physical confounders
raw_evidence.content: The mechanism MeteoSwiss invokes for why burn duration tells you nothing about July is straightforward physics. Each year the pyre is freshly built; the firewood is bought from different suppliers and stored differently, so its moisture content varies. The weather on the festival afternoon - wind, rain, ambient temperature - shifts how flames climb the wood stack. The amount of fire accelerant the guild uses is a direct lever on speed-of-ignition. And the head is packed with about 100 explosive charges whose ignition order depends on how the heat front reaches them. None of these factors carries information about the upcoming June-August jet stream over the Alps, so any correlation that does emerge is dominated by these confounders.

Source: Boeoegg prediction - MeteoSwiss (https://www.meteoswiss.admin.ch/weather/weather-and-climate-from-a-to-z/boeoegg-) Facts: MeteoSwiss's seasonal climate model demonstrates statistically significant correlation with actual summer temperatures - a contrast deliberately drawn against the Boeoegg.

raw_evidence.label: Climate signal: Swiss summers really are getting hotter
raw_evidence.content: Independent of any folk forecast, the Swiss Plateau has warmed measurably over the dataset's time span. MeteoSwiss flags summers above 19 degrees Celsius mean as 'record' years, and the long-term trend is unambiguous in the analyst's own data. The interesting framing is that the snowman is being asked to predict a target that is itself drifting: a 1923 'hot summer' would be a moderate summer today. So the climate signal in the data is real and visible, but it is not the snowman's signal.

raw_evidence.label: Long-run trend in Swiss-Plateau summer temperature
raw_evidence.content: Linear regression over all 67 years gives a slope of +0.0415 deg C per year, r = 0.675, p = 3.81e-10 - a strong, highly significant warming trend. Implied 100-year warming is 4.15 deg C. Comparing the first 30 years on record (1923-1987) with the last 30 years (1995-2025), mean summer temperature rises from 16.67 deg C to 18.53 deg C - a 1.86 deg C gap. So while the snowman fails to predict whether any individual summer is hot, the underlying summers are getting hotter on a schedule.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_10: Linear trend in summer mean temperature 1923-2025 ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
tdf = df.dropna(subset=["tre200m0"]).copy()
slope, intercept, r, p, se = stats.linregress(tdf["year"], tdf["tre200m0"])
print(f"n = {len(tdf)}")
print(f"slope: {slope:.4f} C/year   r = {r:.3f}   p = {p:.2e}")
print(f"100-year warming implied by slope: {slope*100:.2f} C")
# Compare first 30 vs last 30 years
first30 = tdf.head(30)["tre200m0"]
last30 = tdf.tail(30)["tre200m0"]
print(f"first 30 yrs covered ({tdf.head(30)['year'].min()}-{tdf.head(30)['year'].max()}) mean T: {first30.mean():.2f}C")
print(f"last 30 yrs covered ({tdf.tail(30)['year'].min()}-{tdf.tail(30)['year'].max()}) mean T: {last30.mean():.2f}C")
print(f"diff: {last30.mean()-first30.mean():.2f}C")

raw_evidence.label: Long-run trend in Swiss-Plateau summer temperature
raw_evidence.content: Linear regression over all 67 years gives a slope of +0.0415 deg C per year, r = 0.675, p = 3.81e-10 - a strong, highly significant warming trend. Comparing the first 30 years on record (1923-1987) with the last 30 years (1995-2025), mean summer temperature rises from 16.67 deg C to 18.53 deg C - a 1.86 deg C gap. So while the snowman fails to predict whether any individual summer is hot, the underlying summers are getting hotter on a schedule.

print(f"diff: {last30.mean()-first30.mean():.2f}C")

raw_evidence.label: Long-run trend in Swiss-Plateau summer temperature
raw_evidence.content: Linear regression over all 67 years gives a slope of +0.0415 deg C per year, r = 0.675, p = 3.81e-10 - a strong, highly significant warming trend. Implied 100-year warming is 4.15 deg C. Comparing the first 30 years on record (1923-1987) with the last 30 years (1995-2025), mean summer temperature rises from 16.67 deg C to 18.53 deg C - a 1.86 deg C gap. So while the snowman fails to predict whether any individual summer is hot, the underlying summers are getting hotter on a schedule.

# --- ana_10: Linear trend in summer mean temperature 1923-2025 ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
tdf = df.dropna(subset=["tre200m0"]).copy()

print(f"n = {len(tdf)}")
print(f"slope: {slope:.4f} C/year   r = {r:.3f}   p = {p:.2e}")
print(f"100-year warming implied by slope: {slope*100:.2f} C")
# Compare first 30 vs last 30 years
first30 = tdf.head(30)["tre200m0"]
last30 = tdf.tail(30)["tre200m0"]
print(f"first 30 yrs covered ({tdf.head(30)['year'].min()}-{tdf.head(30)['year'].max()}) mean T: {first30.mean():.2f}C")
print(f"last 30 yrs covered ({tdf.tail(30)['year'].min()}-{tdf.tail(30)['year'].max()}) mean T: {last30.mean():.2f}C")
print(f"diff: {last30.mean()-first30.mean():.2f}C")

raw_evidence.label: Record summers by decade
raw_evidence.content: Frequency of record summers (mean >= 19 deg C) by decade reveals an unmistakable acceleration. The 1920s through 1970s contain ZERO record summers across 22 observed years. The 1980s, 1990s and 2000s each contain just 1 record summer in 10 years (10%). The 2010s jump to 4 in 9 years (44.4%). The 2020s already sit at 4 record summers in 6 observed years (66.7%). What used to be a once-a-decade event is now the modal outcome - the climate signal is loud and obvious in the same dataset where the snowman signal is silent.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_13: Counts of record (>=19C) summers by decade ---
print("\n=== ana_13 ===")
tdf2 = df.dropna(subset=["tre200m0"]).copy()
tdf2["decade"] = (tdf2["year"] // 10) * 10
rec_dec = tdf2.groupby("decade")["record"].agg(["sum", "count"]).rename(columns={"sum": "record_yrs", "count": "total_yrs"})
rec_dec["pct"] = (rec_dec["record_yrs"] / rec_dec["total_yrs"] * 100).round(1)
print(rec_dec)

raw_evidence.content: The dataset reproduces every example MeteoSwiss cites. 1974 - shortest burn (5.12 min) - was followed by an unremarkable 16.57 deg C summer; the snowman was wrong. 2003 - second shortest at 5.70 min - was followed by a record-shattering 21.67 deg C summer; the snowman was right but, MeteoSwiss says, by chance. 2022 burned for 37.98 min and the summer hit 20.40 deg C (a record); the snowman was wrong. 2023 burned for a record 57 min, then the summer was 20.07 deg C (a record); the snowman was wrong. Even 2025 burned for 26.50 min, a slow time, and was followed by a 19.60 deg C record summer. Across the eight celebrity years (1974, 2003, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022, 2023, 2025), the folk rule is right once.

# --- ana_09: 2003 vs 2022 vs 2023 - the celebrity case studies ---
